cohort.body_name: Durham Public Schools Board of Education
cohort.label: 2022–2024 School Board
cohort.transition_reason: Swearing-in of May 17, 2022 election winners: Emily Chávez (District 1, succeeding outgoing two-term incumbent Mike Lee), Millicent Rogers (Consolidated District B special election, defeating appointed incumbent Frederick Xavier Ravin III), and re-elected incumbents Bettina Umstead (District 2), Matt Sears (District 3), and Natalie Beyer (District 4). Bettina Umstead continued as Chair; Matt Sears elected Vice Chair. Mid-term resignation of District 3 member and Vice Chair Matt Sears (announced January 31, 2023 to join the Durham Public Schools Foundation as Director of Partnerships), leaving a 6-member board pending appointment of a successor. Appointment (March 16, 2023) and swearing-in (March 23, 2023) of Jessica Carda-Auten to fill the District 3 vacancy left by Matt Sears, restoring the 7-member board. Bettina Umstead continued as Chair; Emily Chávez elected Vice Chair for 2023–2024.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 2/22/24 | Part 2
conflicts.issue: Interim Classified Salary Schedule Option 1 (11% over 2022-23) vs. Honoring October/January Pay or Delaying Implementation
conflicts.summary: The board split 5-2 on adopting Option 1 (restoring 2022-23 salary schedules with an 11% across-the-board increase) for March–June 2024 to stay within the FY24 budget while developing permanent FY25 schedules.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Option 1 (11% increase with 1-to-1 experience steps) now as the fiscally responsible stopgap within existing FY24 funds while exploring one-time relief for the lowest-paid workers and awaiting permanent FY25 proposals.
side_a_arguments: Honoring October letters costs ~$1M/month ($99M annualized), depleting one-time fund balance and risking future July cuts or ESSER cliff layoffs.
Option 1 restores 1-to-1 public and private experience steps and provides certainty for March–June within budgeted revenue.
All 1,875 classified staff remain at least 11% above 2022-23 pay while Comptroller Crutchfield prepares a permanent market-based FY25 plan.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose immediate implementation of Option 1 and protect workers from pay reductions relative to October/January salary letters without 30 days' notice or granular Group 1 impact data.
side_b_arguments: NC State Personnel Manual Section 4.3 requires at least 30 days' written notice before reducing salary or grade.
68–74% of classified workers (including Group 1 staff earning under $43,450) still face lower pay than October letters, without individualized impact details.
One-time sources or further study during March could avoid abrupt pay reductions before a permanent schedule is ready.
conflicts.resolution: Option 1 passed 5-2 on a roll-call vote (02:07:49), alongside board consensus directing staff to investigate one-time bridge assistance for lowest-paid staff and tasking Crutchfield with returning permanent FY25 options in late March.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Meeting | 2/2/24
conflicts.issue: Immediate Adoption of Option 2 (11% Schedule) or Option 1 vs. Tabling Compensation Decision to February 8
conflicts.summary: After Option 2 failed 2-5 and Option 1 died without a second, the board split 4-3 to postpone further compensation action until February 8.
conflicts.side_a_position: Table the compensation decision to February 8 (after rejecting Option 2) so staff and the newly appointed comptroller can provide additional fiscal clarity and avoid rushing into an unpopular cut.
side_a_arguments: Board members felt pressured without full financial health data and wanted time to collaborate with staff, DAE, and the new comptroller.
Payroll could still accommodate a February 8 decision if made early enough.
conflicts.side_b_position: Make an immediate decision on February 2 (supporting Option 1 or opposing further delay) so employees have certainty and are not left in limbo.
side_b_arguments: Delaying another week 'kicks the can down the road' and prolongs employee anxiety and potential school walkouts.
Staff had already provided budgeted options (Option 1 at $91.2M or Option 2 at $90.1M) enabling a timely decision.
conflicts.resolution: Option 2 failed 2-5 (04:43:11) and the motion to table until February 8 carried 4-3 (04:47:36).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 11/16/23
conflicts.issue: Purchase of 4,002 Chromebooks from CDW-G and 1:1 Device Sustainability
conflicts.summary: The board split 5-2 on approving a purchase of 4,002 replacement Chromebooks from CDW-G amid questions over unrecovered devices, recovery incentives, and long-term sustainability once federal ESSER funds expire.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 4,002 Chromebook purchase now to replace damaged devices in students' hands while continuing to evaluate long-term 1:1 sustainability.
side_a_arguments: Replacement devices are needed immediately to swap out broken or damaged student Chromebooks while harvesting salvageable parts.
District loss rates align with peer districts (~5%) and administration can return with budget sustainability recommendations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the Chromebook purchase pending stronger device recovery accountability, parent portal transparency, and budget/program clarity.
side_b_arguments: 1,221 devices remain assigned to students no longer enrolled in DPS, and families lack online visibility into which devices were issued to their children.
Spending budget dollars on recovery incentives ('bribing back' devices) before exhausting direct recovery requests is concerning.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to purchase 4,002 Chromebooks from CDW-G passed 5-2; staff committed to bringing back long-term 1:1 sustainability recommendations.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 2/8/24
conflicts.issue: Adopting Option 4 (15% Increase Starting March) Immediately vs. Waiting for Comptroller Analysis and Funding Clarity
conflicts.summary: Following a unanimous vote to maintain October pay rates for February, the board split 3-4 rejecting Jovonia Lewis's motion to adopt Option 4 (15% raise over 2022-23 starting March) and then voted 5-2 to postpone March–June decisions until February 22.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Option 4 (15% increase with 1-to-1 steps) immediately to end employee anxiety, restore years of experience, and identify ~$2M in one-time funds/fund balance.
side_a_arguments: Leaving employees in limbo damages mental health and risks further school closures and staff departures.
Option 4 honors years of experience at 1-to-1 and ensures every classified employee receives at least 15% over 2022-23.
The ~$2M difference could be covered from fund balance or budget savings while seeking recurring county funds next year.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold off on deciding March–June salary schedules until Comptroller Kerry Crutchfield, CFO Ojijo, and staff provide full fiscal health data, funding sources, and individual employee impact examples.
side_b_arguments: Board lacked complete data on how Option 4 would affect the 567 employees still below October pay, ESSER-funded 113 positions expiring, and declining ADM.
Fund balance had already dropped from ~$11M to $6.4M against a $12.7M target, and staff should not spend unverified funds before comptroller review.
Waiting until February 22 allows administration to model 11%, 12%, and 15% options and share concrete examples with staff.
conflicts.resolution: Option 4 failed 3-4 on roll call (02:48:54), and the board voted 5-2 to postpone March–June compensation decisions to February 22 with board proposals due February 13 (03:04:02).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 6/15/23
conflicts.issue: Renewal of 22-SRO Contract with Durham County Sheriff's Office for SY 2023-24
conflicts.summary: The board split 4-2 on renewing the existing School Resource Officer MOU unchanged for another school year versus withholding approval until task force reforms and stronger training/grievance accountability were added.
conflicts.side_a_position: Renew the 2023-24 SRO MOU now (and seek funding for Lakeview) while awaiting the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force's October 2023 recommendations for 2024-25.
side_a_arguments: Year-round schools open in July, requiring an active MOU so campus safety coverage does not lapse.
The Community Safety and Wellness Task Force has conducted 16 listening sessions and should finalize its recommendations before major structural changes are negotiated.
Adding an SRO at Lakeview addresses campus weapon and coverage gaps if county funding is secured.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose renewing the MOU unchanged due to concerns over policing in schools, lack of grievance/referral data, and inability to incorporate task force reforms until 2024-25.
side_b_arguments: Increased law enforcement in schools may not support the educational process, and alternative non-SRO models (such as Milwaukee) merit evaluation.
Board members had not yet received requested data on SRO grievances, discipline/law enforcement referrals, or mandatory Youth Mental Health First Aid training.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-2 on roll call to extend the SRO MOU for SY 2023-24 while committing to review task force recommendations once released.

conflicts.meeting_title: DPS Board of Education -District 3 Candidate Selection
conflicts.issue: Selection of District 3 Board Vacancy Appointee (Jessica Carda-Auten vs. Kevin Primus)
conflicts.summary: The six seated board members split 4-2 in selecting a District 3 appointee to serve through June 30, 2024, dividing between public health researcher and PTA parent Jessica Carda-Auten and community advocate/researcher Kevin Primus.
conflicts.side_a_position: Appoint Jessica Carda-Auten based on her public health expertise, DPS parent and PTA involvement, collaborative demeanor, and readiness for Growing Together.
side_a_arguments: Carda-Auten brings public health and data-driven expertise, strong relationships with educators, principals, and county commissioners, and deep investment as a DPS parent.
Her collaborative listening style across differences equips the board to navigate tough Growing Together redistricting conversations and eliminate the school-to-prison pipeline.
conflicts.side_b_position: Appoint Kevin Primus for his urgency on youth violence, focus on trauma-informed/EC/ELL metrics, and broad community coalition support.
side_b_arguments: Primus demonstrated data-driven focus on EC, ELL, and trauma-informed training alongside broad research connections (Mayo Clinic, Duke, UC Davis) and community accountability amid ongoing youth gun violence.
Community leaders and coalition signatories rallied strongly behind his candidacy.
conflicts.resolution: Kevin Primus's nomination failed 2-4 and Jessica Carda-Auten's nomination passed 4-2 on roll call votes.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 4/25/24
conflicts.issue: Targeted $200/Month EC & ESL Teacher Supplement vs. Broader $1.5M Flexible Hard-to-Staff Equity Pool
conflicts.summary: Board members debated whether to mandate an immediate $200/month flat supplement restricted to certified EC and ESL teachers or allocate a larger, flexible $1.5 million hard-to-staff pot informed by staffing equity data.
conflicts.side_a_position: Guarantee an explicit $200/month supplement for EC and ESL teachers immediately in the proposed budget.
side_a_arguments: Honors sustained public advocacy from DAE, EC parents, and ESL educators facing severe vacancy crises.
Establishes a concrete floor for two highest-need classroom teacher groups without further delay.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize a flexible $1.5 million hard-to-staff equity plan guided by administration data rather than locking in an ad hoc single-role supplement.
side_b_arguments: Excludes EC instructional assistants, therapists, nurses, and other hard-to-fill staff if restricted solely to certified EC/ESL teachers.
Adding non-reimbursable local supplements late in the budget process risks unintended inequities across employee groups.
conflicts.resolution: The Board passed both measures in sequence: first approving the $200/month EC/ESL teacher supplement (7-0) and then approving a $1.5 million hard-to-staff equity plan inclusive of the EC/ESL supplement (6-0).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 3/21/24
conflicts.issue: Superintendent Search Firm Selection: Alma Advisory Group vs. North Carolina School Boards Association (NCSBA)
conflicts.summary: Board members divided over hiring Alma Advisory Group versus NCSBA based on equity-focused recruitment capacity, cost, timeline feasibility, and administrative burden.
conflicts.side_a_position: Select Alma Advisory Group for its proactive equity-centered recruitment, cultural competency, and community engagement approach.
side_a_arguments: Alma actively recruits non-traditional and diverse leaders rather than relying on standard passive pools.
Community engagement and competency-based rubrics align strongly with Durham's priorities and rebuilding trust.
conflicts.side_b_position: Favor NCSBA or reject Alma due to higher cost, timeline/staffing burdens, and concerns over prior familiarity.
side_b_arguments: Jovonia Lewis cited NCSBA's lower cost, established North Carolina statutory expertise, and reliable timeline execution.
Alexandra Valladares criticized Alma's cost, lack of a clear roadmap/staff burden clarity, and perceived familiarity/bias concerns.
conflicts.resolution: After tabling for closed-session contract consultation, the Board voted 6-1 at 07:36:13 to select Alma Advisory Group and authorize contract negotiations.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Meeting | 2/15/24
conflicts.issue: Composition and Representation of the Meet and Confer Ad Hoc Working Group
conflicts.summary: Board members and DAE leaders disagreed over whether the Meet and Confer drafting committee should give equal seats to non-union staff (4 DAE / 4 non-DAE) or reflect DAE's union organizing base with a majority or exclusive DAE seat allocation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Include equal employee seats (4 DAE and 4 non-DAE employees alongside 2 administrators and 2 board members + 1 alternate) so all 5,000+ staff have representation.
side_a_arguments: Transportation mechanics, fleet maintenance, and lot managers walked out of the meeting feeling unrepresented by DAE.
An inclusive Durham model should not grant exclusive pay-to-play status to one dues-paying organization over non-members.
Board policy allows the chair to appoint inclusive advisory committees representing diverse job classifications.
conflicts.side_b_position: Grant DAE a majority or exclusive employee seat allocation (e.g., 6 DAE / 2 other, or 8 DAE) rather than an equal 4-4 split with unorganized appointees.
side_b_arguments: DAE drafted the policy, represents roughly 3,000–4,000 workers through democratic organizing committees, and already consults non-members.
Appointing four individual non-DAE employees lacks a democratic accountability structure to a broader worker base.
Carda-Auten floated a 5-3 compromise while Chávez favored 6-2 or 8 DAE to honor DAE's organizing.
conflicts.resolution: The 4 DAE / 4 non-DAE composition passed 6-1 by show of hands (03:24:52), and the board unanimously accelerated member appointments to February 22 (03:37:04).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 10/12/23
conflicts.issue: Approving Classified Compensation Study Without Prior Public Salary Schedule Posting
conflicts.summary: The board split 6-1 over approving the classified compensation study immediately to preserve October payroll versus tabling the vote until concrete salary schedules could be posted publicly for transparency.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the compensation study immediately with a requirement that full salary schedules be posted and presented publicly at the October 26 meeting.
side_a_arguments: CFO Paul LeSieur stated payroll had already been held up for days and waiting until Monday would jeopardize employees' end-of-month paychecks.
Adding a requirement to bring concrete salary schedule documentation back on October 26 ensures public transparency without hurting workers' pay.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approving the compensation study before concrete salary schedule documents are posted publicly for clarity and transparency.
side_b_arguments: Board members and the public lacked a concrete posted schedule clarifying exactly what was being approved.
conflicts.resolution: Amended motion passed 6-1 on roll call; salary schedules were brought back as an open-session agenda update on October 26, 2023.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 5/18/23
conflicts.issue: Continuation vs. Termination of Gaggle Student Device Surveillance Contract
conflicts.summary: The board split 6-1 over terminating DPS's Gaggle monitoring contract effective June 30, 2023 and returning $116,371 in state grant funds versus keeping the software through its 2024 grant end as an added suicide-prevention layer.
conflicts.side_a_position: Terminate the Gaggle contract effective June 30, 2023 and invest effort in relationship-building, 988/tip lines, and student-centered mental health supports.
side_a_arguments: Survey and 100-day metrics did not clearly distinguish where Gaggle prevented harm versus created harm, with many PSS alerts turning out to be non-emergencies and staff spending significant after-hours time.
Gaggle raised serious student privacy concerns, chilled students from logging into school accounts on personal devices, and lacked transparent auditing for algorithmic bias.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain Gaggle through the remainder of its grant-funded term in 2024 until an alternative safety net is established.
side_b_arguments: Gaggle provides an extra protective layer against rising youth suicidal ideation and self-harm, and 75% of surveyed contacts reported taking action on at least one safety concern they would not have otherwise known.
Returning the funds leaves a gap before additional counselors or replacement supports are in place.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1 on roll call authorizing administration to terminate the Gaggle contract effective June 30, 2023.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 5/18/23
conflicts.issue: Strategic Plan Specificity on Exceptional Children (EC) Metrics and Culturally Responsive Curriculum
conflicts.summary: Board members debated how explicitly the five-year Strategic Plan goals should single out EC students, EC educators, and culturally responsive curriculum versus keeping high-level goals flexible.
conflicts.side_a_position: Add explicit EC student/educator benchmarks to Goal 1B/3A-3B and elevate 'Culturally Responsive Curriculum' as a headline strategy title.
side_a_arguments: Goal 1B explicitly broke out Black, Hispanic, and LEP students while omitting EC students, risking lower visibility and accountability for students with disabilities.
Renamings such as 'Culturally Responsive Curriculum' signal clear district values amid hostile state-level curriculum politics.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the high-level five-year strategic plan broad enough to remain adaptable across changing staffing shortages and avoid locking departments into narrow operational metrics.
side_b_arguments: Over-specifying single hard-to-fill roles or narrow metrics at the 30,000-foot level could lock the district in over a five-year horizon, whereas department work plans and monthly updates track disaggregated data.
Opportunity Gaps is broader than curriculum alone and already encompasses culturally responsive curriculum, teacher diversity, and discipline.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved unanimously (7-0) by adopting the plan with a directive for staff and RTI to add an appropriate EC metric in consultation with the EC department and strengthen identity-inclusion wording.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Meeting | 1/19/23
conflicts.issue: Immediate Approval vs. One-Week Delay of Growing Together Elementary Assignment Rules
conflicts.summary: Board members broadly supported Growing Together's long-term equity goals but split over whether to adopt the elementary assignment rules immediately on January 19 ahead of the February 6 magnet application deadline or delay one week to publish written FAQs, regional maps, and school-specific answers for families and teachers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Growing Together elementary rules immediately so families and principals have definitive rules before the February 6 magnet window closes
side_a_arguments: Implementation does not take effect until 2024-25 (18 months away), and delaying one week would not change the underlying plan while shortening notice before the February 6 magnet lottery deadline.
Administrators and principals needed formal board authorization to publish concrete, address-specific communications, geocoded tools, and school-level outreach.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay the vote until written FAQs and clear transition details for sunsetting magnets and staff are published to rebuild community trust
side_b_arguments: Board members and families—especially at Club Boulevard, R.N. Harris, Sandy Ridge, and Little River—still had unanswered questions about sunsetting magnets, fourth/fifth grade transfer rules, sibling rules, and teacher transfers.
Voting before publishing written FAQs risked deepening distrust and accelerating teacher and family departures.
conflicts.resolution: Natalie Beyer voiced support for a one-week delay during debate and requested a straw poll, then ultimately voted Aye alongside Umstead, Lewis, Valladares, Chávez, and Sears to pass the rules 6-1, with Millicent Rogers casting the sole Nay vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Called Meeting | 5/13/24
conflicts.issue: Publicly Named Finalist Visits (Option A) vs. Confidential NDA Community Panels (Option B)
conflicts.summary: Board members debated whether superintendent finalists should be publicly announced for open community forums (Option A) or interviewed in closed sessions with confidential community stakeholder panels signing non-disclosure agreements (Option B).
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold an open public finalist round so all Durham stakeholders can vet and engage finalists transparently.
side_a_arguments: Public forums help rebuild community trust after recent district turmoil.
Board leadership originally signaled openness and broad community participation in finalist vetting.
conflicts.side_b_position: Use confidential finalist community panels under signed NDAs without publicly naming non-selected finalists.
side_b_arguments: Two current applicants and a prospective sitting superintendent expressed discomfort with public finalist exposure.
Sitting superintendents will withdraw if unsuccessful finalist applications jeopardize their current jobs.
A 10-to-12-person representative community panel under NDAs still incorporates student, parent, and educator perspectives.
conflicts.resolution: Millicent Rogers amended her original motion (accepted by seconder Emily Chávez) to adopt Option B—confidential finalist panels with signed confidentiality agreements and no public release of finalist names—passing 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 4/11/24
conflicts.issue: Focusing the Draft Legislative Agenda on Targeted Regional Priorities vs. Comprehensive Equity Advocacy
conflicts.summary: Following presentation of the five-bucket draft Legislative Agenda, members debated whether to narrow the asks to fewer targeted priorities coordinated with Wake and Chapel Hill-Carrboro boards or retain the broad set of priorities ahead of the Durham legislative delegation meeting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Narrow and target the legislative asks and coordinate explicitly with neighboring districts so priority issues gain traction.
side_a_arguments: If the Board focuses on everything, it risks focusing on nothing during a short legislative session.
Joint asks backed by Wake and Orange/Chapel Hill-Carrboro carry greater collective weight in Raleigh.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain a comprehensive equity-rooted agenda (caps on EC/ELL, K-3 TA funding, Pre-K, Growing Together, local supplement equity) while aligning where possible with NCSBA and neighboring districts.
side_b_arguments: Many items already align with Chapel Hill-Carrboro, Wake County, and NCSBA priorities.
Lifting arbitrary state EC/ELL caps, restoring K-3 instructional assistant funding, and funding local supplement equity cannot be left off the record.
conflicts.resolution: Members agreed to leave the document as a draft for presentation to the Durham delegation on April 17 and bring a finalized version back for a formal vote on April 25.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Meeting | 4/4/24
conflicts.issue: Approval of $89,500 Alma Advisory Group Superintendent Search Contract and Pre-Vote Transparency
conflicts.summary: The board split 4-3 over contracting with Alma Advisory Group for $89,500 to lead the superintendent search, balancing cost concerns and pre-vote contract transparency against community engagement and candidate sourcing priorities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $89,500 Alma Advisory Group contract to lead nationwide recruitment and community engagement for the next superintendent.
side_a_arguments: Selecting a superintendent is the board's most consequential investment, and Alma brings strong community-building and equity context.
Alma's role is strictly to bring a strong candidate pool while the board retains decision-making authority.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the $89,500 contract due to cost, competing vendors' language capabilities, and lack of pre-vote public posting.
side_b_arguments: Cost-effectiveness is critical given the district's historical inability to pay classified staff as desired, and competing firms offered robust language access (including nine simultaneous languages) at different price points.
Legal counsel confirmed contracts are often attached to agendas as public records prior to approval, whereas this final contract was only being released after the vote.
conflicts.resolution: Contract approved 4-3 by voice/hand vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 8/10/23
conflicts.issue: Design, Metrics, and Timeline for Black and Hispanic Student Achievement Plan Resolution
conflicts.summary: Board members and Superintendent Dr. Mubenga differed over adopting the draft Black and Hispanic Student Achievement resolution as written versus refining its alignment with the Strategic Plan, Family Advisory Council structure, and realistic reporting cadence.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move forward urgently with an explicit resolution, frequent deliverables, and a dedicated Family Advisory Council focused on Black and Hispanic students.
side_a_arguments: Black and Hispanic students make up roughly 80% of DPS and require urgent, explicit accountability beyond general strategic plan language.
An explicit Family Advisory Council and more frequent deliverables will strengthen community trust and oversight.
conflicts.side_b_position: Take several weeks to align metrics with annual data availability, incorporate existing parent advisory structures and ESL/immigrant language, and ensure realistic timelines.
side_b_arguments: Annual state assessment metrics cannot change meaningfully on a quarterly cadence, and December 2023 turnaround is too compressed for authentic council recruitment.
The resolution should explicitly align with Strategic Plan Goals 1B, 2B, and 3C and acknowledge immigrant/ESL students without duplicating staff workload.
conflicts.resolution: No vote taken; board reached consensus for Millicent Rogers and a colleague to work with Superintendent Mubenga's team on a revised draft for the September work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 6/15/23
conflicts.issue: Growing Together Secondary Plan and Sunsetting High School Grades at School for Creative Studies
conflicts.summary: The board split 4-2 over adopting the Growing Together secondary boundary and program plan, centered on converting School for Creative Studies (SCS) from a 6-12 campus into a 6-8 year-round middle school.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the Growing Together secondary plan converting SCS to a 6-8 year-round middle school to relieve northern/eastern growth and serve more middle schoolers.
side_a_arguments: Rapid residential growth in northern and eastern Durham requires expanding middle school year-round capacity near Holt, Eno Valley/Easley, and Oak Grove.
SCS's creative theme remains intact for grades 6-8, while the 5-year review rule allows revisiting high school options later.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject sunsetting SCS's high school program because it serves neurodivergent and diverse learners as the district's only year-round high school.
side_b_arguments: SCS is the only year-round middle/high magnet in North Carolina and provides a small, supportive environment where struggling and neurodivergent students thrive.
Alternative land utilization or retrofitting on the Red Mill Road campus was not sufficiently explored before deciding to phase out grades 9-12.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-2 on roll call to adopt the Growing Together secondary plan.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 2/9/23
conflicts.issue: Election of Board Vice Chair and Board Communication/Leadership Process
conflicts.summary: Following Matt Sears's resignation, the board split 3-3 across two rounds between nominees Emily Chávez and Jovonia Lewis amid pointed debate over rotational leadership, prior experience, and alleged cliques/exclusionary communication before Chair Bettina Umstead broke the tie for Chávez on the third ballot.
conflicts.side_a_position: Elect Emily Chávez as Vice Chair to bring new energy, rotational leadership, and collaborative focus
side_a_arguments: Chávez brought budget advisory co-chair experience, an intersectional equity lens, and strong relationships with commissioners and colleagues.
Supporting Chávez aligned with rotational leadership and moving the board's agenda forward after two deadlocked ballots.
conflicts.side_b_position: Elect Jovonia Lewis based on three years of board experience and push back against perceived pre-arranged cliques and exclusionary communication
side_b_arguments: Lewis argued that after three years on the board—including pandemic leadership and prior service—experience and transparency should outweigh experimentation, noting Beyer had previously said she lacked experience in her first year.
Valladares criticized perceived pre-arranged whip counts, side meetings with partners like the DPS Foundation and Self-Help, and inequitable communication excluding certain board members.
conflicts.resolution: After Round 1 (Chávez) and Round 2 (Lewis) both tied 3-3, Bettina Umstead switched from voting against both nominees to voting Aye for Emily Chávez in Round 3, electing Chávez 4-2; Valladares requested Policy Committee review of Policy 220 officer terms.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Meeting | 4/10/24
conflicts.issue: Board Liaison Structure and North Carolina Open Meetings Law Compliance
conflicts.summary: Board members and counsel debated whether designating two board members as interim liaisons to Alma Advisory Group posed legal risks under Open Meetings Law or concentrated influence compared to routing communications solely through the Chair.
conflicts.side_a_position: Allow two board liaisons (or open interest across members) with clear guardrails to ensure broader representation and backup capacity.
side_a_arguments: Two liaisons provide continuity if one member has scheduling conflicts.
Allowing other interested members—including outgoing members like Alexandra Valladares—prevents concentrating search communication solely in the Chair and Vice Chair.
conflicts.side_b_position: Limit interim point-of-contact duties to the Chair (or Chair/Vice Chair) or defer liaison selection to avoid Open Meetings Law complications and premature decisions.
side_b_arguments: Chair typically handles routine vendor logistics and polling under board practice without needing a separate subcommittee.
Attorney Bloomberg noted legal review is prudent if multiple members act on behalf of the Board between noticed meetings.
conflicts.resolution: Per Millicent Rogers's and Alexandra Valladares's suggestion, the Board held off naming formal liaisons that evening and asked Chair Bettina Umstead and Vice Chair Emily Chávez to check individually with board members ahead of the next meeting (resolved April 11 with Chair and Vice Chair serving as points of contact).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 3/21/24
conflicts.issue: Postponing Growing Together and Transportation Presentations vs. Hearing Waiting Staff and Community
conflicts.summary: Around 11:00 PM (video timestamp 04:08:29), board members split 5-1 over whether to defer Growing Together and Transportation presentations to the April work session.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move Growing Together and Transportation presentations to the April 11 work session so they receive adequate, unhurried discussion.
side_a_arguments: Addressing complex redistricting and transportation updates near midnight prevents meaningful dialogue.
Deferring to April allows staff to present updated April lottery data.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep Growing Together on the March 21 agenda because families and staff waited hours to hear the update.
side_b_arguments: With spring break and transfer windows underway, community members in the room expected immediate answers.
side_b_members: Unspecified dissenting member (1 Nay on 5-1 vote)
conflicts.resolution: Motion to amend the agenda and move both presentations to the April 11 work session passed 5-1 at 04:28:45.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Meeting | 2/2/24
conflicts.issue: Scope of Meet and Confer Engagement: DAE-Led vs. Broad Cross-Section of Educators and Parents
conflicts.summary: Board members debated whether the proposed Meet and Confer conversation should start specifically with DAE leadership or explicitly encompass non-DAE advocacy groups, non-union educators, and parents.
conflicts.side_a_position: Invite a broad cross-section of current DPS educators, PTAs, parent advocates, and multiple groups alongside DAE to avoid giving exclusive preference to one dues-charging organization.
side_a_arguments: Not all DPS employees belong to DAE, and parents/PTAs and non-union groups are also impacted by district decisions.
Starting on the right foot requires avoiding 'pay-to-play' perception and external organizers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Begin the initial public conversation with DAE leadership—who brought the Meet and Confer proposal—while keeping the meeting open to the public and discussing broader inclusion together.
side_b_arguments: DAE brought the policy proposal and represents thousands of DPS workers.
Every board meeting is public by law, and the group can determine broader participation rules once convened.
conflicts.resolution: Board initiated a roll-call vote at 05:43:52 on Rogers's motion to send a doodle poll for an open meeting with DAE leadership (audio cut out before final tally, though the meeting subsequently occurred on Feb 15).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 4/6/23
conflicts.issue: Day of Remembrance Proposal: Concrete Policy Commitments and Age-Appropriateness vs. Community Vigil
conflicts.summary: Board members clashed sharply over whether a proposed May 15 Day of Remembrance risked being 'performative' or triggering for younger students versus serving as an essential, community-requested acknowledgment of grief.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require concrete violence-prevention policies and ensure age-appropriate school implementation rather than holding a performative event or district-wide moments of silence for young children.
side_a_arguments: The board should pair any remembrance with actionable preventative measures such as SAVE clubs and public health/gun-control advocacy rather than a performative day alone.
District-wide moments of silence in elementary and middle schools may not be age-appropriate, and City Council/BOCC partners needed fuller readiness.
conflicts.side_b_position: Honor families' explicit requests for collective mourning and visibility while building joint action steps through a tri-body resolution.
side_b_arguments: Calling community-initiated mourning and vigils 'performative' dismissed real family grief and felt like a microaggression to organizers.
A joint resolution with City Council and County Commissioners can both validate community trauma and commit to concrete youth programs, summer jobs, and prevention work.
conflicts.resolution: Board formed a working committee of Jovonia Lewis, Millicent Rogers, and Alexandra Valladares to draft an action-oriented tri-body resolution with student support guidance for April 20.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Called Meeting | 4/18/24
conflicts.issue: Strict Minimum Experience Criteria vs. Broad Desired Qualifications in Superintendent Job Profile
conflicts.summary: During the job profile review, board members debated how strictly to frame required prior experience—specifically whether requiring leadership in a district 'as large and complex as DPS' or labeling criteria as 'minimum qualifications' would narrow the applicant pool.
conflicts.side_a_position: Replace 'Minimum' with 'Desired Qualifications' and remove 'as large and complex as DPS' to avoid deterring strong equity-centered or non-traditional leaders.
side_a_arguments: Rigid minimum checkboxes can disproportionately screen out strong candidates of color and leaders from mid-sized or comparable systems.
Desired qualifications give the Board discretion to evaluate holistic competency during screening.
conflicts.side_b_position: Ensure the job profile maintains rigorous operational, financial, and district-scale leadership standards.
side_b_arguments: Candidates must understand complex public district governance, school finance, and rebuilding community trust at DPS's scale.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved through consensus edits revising 'Minimum' to 'Desired Qualifications' while retaining rigorous competency expectations for finance, equity, and district leadership; approved 6-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 3/21/24
conflicts.issue: Impacts of Districtwide Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) Rollout on Title I School Allocations
conflicts.summary: Following staff's recommendation to apply for districtwide free breakfast and lunch under CEP, Alexandra Valladares and administration exchanged contrasting perspectives on five schools losing Title I status.
conflicts.side_a_position: Highlight the 'Tale of Two Cities' nuance that shifting Title I identification strips flexible Title I staffing/Pre-K dollars from five schools (Creekside, Mangum, Club Boulevard, Morehead, George Watts).
side_a_arguments: Removing Title I status eliminates funds principals used to supplement positions like community schools coordinators and Pre-K IAs.
Acknowledged federal lowering of the CEP threshold from 40% to 25% made districtwide CEP newly feasible this year rather than blaming staff for past inaction.
conflicts.side_b_position: Clarify that the five schools' Title I exit is driven independently by declining ISP poverty percentages below 35%, not by adopting districtwide CEP.
side_b_arguments: Those five schools were exiting grandfathering regardless of CEP because their direct-certification ISP dropped below federal Title I thresholds.
Districtwide CEP saves ~$1.5M in nutrition operations, eliminates meal debt, and brings in federal reimbursements while preserving rank-ordered Title I equity.
conflicts.resolution: Administration clarified the Title I grandfathering mechanics and received Board consensus support to proceed with the districtwide CEP application (no formal vote required).

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 11/2/23
conflicts.issue: Navigating SB 49 Policy Updates vs. Non-Compliance and Staff Guidance Timing
conflicts.summary: While board members unanimously advanced six SB 49-aligned policies to a second reading, the discussion exposed sharp tensions over complying with a state law members viewed as harmful, whether staff guidance should precede policy adoption, and public demands for outright non-compliance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay or refuse policy changes until January or until staff procedures and protections are ready, avoiding endorsement of harmful state mandates.
side_a_arguments: Public commenters urged DPS to defy SB 49 and keep existing LGBTQIA+ protections intact.

Jessica Carda-Auten expressed reluctance to amend policies before or without simultaneous administrative guidance for teachers, and Emily Chávez criticized SB 49's K-4 restrictions and forced student outing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Advance the policy revisions and adopt accompanying administrative procedures so staff are not left in legal jeopardy or an ambiguous 'no man's land'.
side_b_arguments: Counsel Mr. Malone advised that SB 49's instructional and notice rules are already state law regardless of local board policy, and asking staff to break the law risks harming employees.
Staff noted formal procedures cannot be issued until the board adopts the underlying policies, and without clear procedures individual schools could act inconsistently.
conflicts.resolution: Board voted unanimously to bring the six policies back for second reading on November 16 while directing staff to prepare accompanying procedures and training timelines by that date.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 8/10/23
conflicts.issue: Whether to Impose a Hard Per-Student Dollar Cap on School Incentive Funds
conflicts.summary: Board members disagreed on whether the $20-per-student school funding allocation should include a strict dollar ceiling per award or rely on School Improvement Teams and equity guidance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Establish explicit per-student dollar limits on student incentive awards comparable to teacher appreciation gift limits.
side_a_arguments: Past high-dollar items such as $300 awards, expensive jackets, or gaming consoles create inequities with staff gift limits and difficult family situations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Rely on the new Office of Equity and Professional Development guidance plus SIT and principal-supervisor review rather than rigid spending caps.
side_b_arguments: Rigid caps could overly restrict school improvement teams from funding meaningful group incentives and educational field trips.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 7-0 without a formal dollar cap, with staff asked to clarify field-trip guidelines and consider earlier June approval for year-round schools.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Work Session | 5/9/24
conflicts.issue: Immediate Pre-K–3 Short-Term Suspension Ban vs. Phased On-Ramp and Task Force Review
conflicts.summary: Following sobering 2022-23 discipline data showing a 7.9% overall short-term suspension rate and 15% rate for students with disabilities, Jovonia Lewis urged drafting a policy ban on Pre-K–3 short-term suspensions before the new school year, while Deputy Superintendent Dr. Nicholas King and other board members favored building supportive alternatives and convening a Code of Conduct Task Force first.
conflicts.side_a_position: Direct staff immediately to draft a policy eliminating short-term out-of-school suspensions for Pre-K through third grade before the 2024-25 school year starts.
side_a_arguments: Some elementary principals already refrain from suspending young children while others continue doing so, creating inequitable outcomes across schools.
Waiting for a full task force risks starting another school year under inconsistent practices.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid an immediate outright ban without first equipping school staff with training, structures, and a multi-stakeholder Policy 4301 task force.
side_b_arguments: Deputy Superintendent Dr. Nicholas King cited research indicating districts that imposed immediate bans without trained alternatives experienced worse outcomes.
Bettina Umstead and Emily Chávez favored an 'additive and subtractive' on-ramp that installs restorative supports alongside forming a Code of Conduct Task Force by June to convene in August.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; Chair Bettina Umstead agreed to work with staff to return with a proposed timeline and framework for the Policy 4301 task force and supportive practices.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 4/25/24
conflicts.issue: Formal Board Approval vs. Informal Modeling Direction for Classified Salary Min/Max Ranges
conflicts.summary: Following Comptroller Carrie Crutchfield's classified salary range presentation, members disagreed on whether the Board should take a formal vote endorsing conceptual pay ranges.
conflicts.side_a_position: Do not take a formal vote on preliminary salary ranges that could create false expectations or confusion before county funding is known.
side_a_arguments: Public and staff still have unresolved questions about individual placement and neighboring district comparisons.
Formal votes on preliminary concepts risk repeating the October salary rollout miscommunication.
conflicts.side_b_position: Give staff clear board direction on pay-range width so modeling and individualized pay notices can proceed.
side_b_arguments: Staff need guidance on 45% to 55% range assumptions to prepare modeling for employees ahead of county budget negotiations.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved at 02:56:03 through informal thumbs-up consensus directing staff to model 45% to 55% ranges without taking a formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Work Session | 3/7/24
conflicts.issue: Funding Once-a-Week Elementary World Language Classes vs. Shifting Resources to Dual Language Immersion, EC/ESL Supplements, and CEP
conflicts.summary: During FY 2024-25 budget priority discussions, Vice Chair Emily Chávez argued against investing in once-a-week elementary World Language expansion—contending it benefits non-Latinx students disproportionately—while other members defended World Language equity alongside exploring EC/ESL/bilingual supplements and districtwide CEP.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reconsider costly once-a-week elementary World Language staffing and instead prioritize Dual Language Immersion (DLI), EC/ESL/bilingual staff investments, and outcomes for Black, Latinx, EC, and low-SES students.
side_a_arguments: Once-a-week World Language classes do not create true bilingualism like DLI and may primarily benefit non-Latinx peers.
Resources should center marginalized students—Black, Latinx, EC, and ESL learners—and representation of teachers of color.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain neighborhood school World Language equity and Universal Pre-K commitments while simultaneously gathering cost estimates for EC/ESL/bilingual supplements and districtwide CEP.
side_b_arguments: Natalie Beyer noted districtwide CEP and Universal Pre-K belong in county budget asks alongside program evaluations.
Bettina Umstead urged keeping Growing Together equity commitments while requesting concrete cost proposals for EC IAs/certified/classified staff, bilingual stipends, and universal CEP.
conflicts.resolution: Members agreed to await program evaluation data on World Language and DLI while directing administration to bring back cost estimates for EC supplements, bilingual staff stipends, and universal CEP at the next meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 11/17/22
conflicts.issue: Procedural Process vs. Immediate First-Reading Adoption of Draft LGBTQ+ Gender Support Policy
conflicts.summary: Board members debated whether to vote immediately on a member-drafted LGBTQ+ policy on first reading or follow formal agenda-notice procedures by directing staff and legal counsel to bring a vetted Orange County-model policy to the next meeting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance a foundational policy immediately rather than waiting for task force completion or further delay.
side_a_arguments: Community families have advocated for months and expect visible leadership to put a baseline policy in the policy manual.
Policies adapted from Orange and Buncombe counties are already vetted and reviewed by members and can be revised later as a living document.
Passing a formal directive ensures accountability rather than relying on informal expectations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Follow formal governance notice procedures and clarify whether administration is revising existing Gender Support Guidelines or drafting a new policy before voting.
side_b_arguments: The item was added to the agenda solely for discussion, not as a posted action item or first reading for public notice.
Passing policy without a finalized document posted on the agenda ahead of time departs from the board's governance and policy-committee process.
Board Attorney Rod Malone recommended directing staff and counsel to bring a reviewed draft to the next meeting, when the board could waive second reading if satisfied.
conflicts.resolution: The board reached consensus and voted 7-0 on Alexandra Valladares's motion (seconded by Natalie Beyer) directing administration to bring an LGBTQ+ gender support policy based on the Orange County model to the next board meeting, paired with a time-limited task force.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Meeting | 3/13/24
conflicts.issue: Conflict-of-Interest Scrutiny, Political Ties, and Microaggression Dispute During Search Firm Screening
conflicts.summary: A sharp disagreement arose when Alexandra Valladares questioned perceived political and local connections among search firm bidders—specifically referencing Durham City Council Member Javiera Caballero's former work at Alma Advisory Group—prompting pushback from Natalie Beyer over singling out firms and culminating in a point of personal privilege.
conflicts.side_a_position: Examine political, elected-official, and local connections across search firms transparently to avoid conflicts of interest or public mistrust.
side_a_arguments: Community trust requires scrutinizing whether elected officials or former Durham consultants have ties to bidding firms such as Alma, alongside noting staff ties to NCSBA.
Dismissing these transparency concerns as a 'conspiracy theory' constitutes a microaggression rather than addressing legitimate governance questions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Apply neutral conflict-of-interest standards evenly across all bidders without singling out one firm or relying on speculation.
side_b_arguments: Legal conflict thresholds (such as statutory 10% ownership/family rules cited by Attorney Rod Malone) govern disqualifications, and multiple firms have former public education connections.
Speculative claims about one firm risk tainting the RFP review unfairly.
conflicts.resolution: Following Valladares's point of personal privilege, Natalie Beyer apologized at 00:40:49 for the phrase used, Attorney Rod Malone clarified statutory conflict thresholds, and the Board agreed by consensus at 00:44:37 to bar any vendor communications outside designated contact Dr. Tanya Giovanni before shortlisting NCSBA, Alma, BWP, and Summit.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Public Hearing for Policy 1310 | 11/9/23
conflicts.issue: Draft Policy 1310 (Parental Engagement) Alignment with SB 49 vs. LGBTQIA+ Student Protections
conflicts.summary: Public hearing speakers split sharply over whether Draft Policy 1310 went too far in accommodating classroom discussions and opt-out exceptions relative to SB 49 or went too far in complying with state mandates that require parental pronoun notifications and restrict K-4 gender/sexuality instruction.
conflicts.side_a_position: Align Policy 1310 strictly and clearly with all SB 49 (Parents' Bill of Rights) statutory mandates.
side_a_arguments: SB 49 applies statewide across all 100 counties regardless of local opposition.

Draft Policy 1310 omits explicit parental consent rules for healthcare clinics (e.g., Hillside High), allows marketing/opt-out and short-duration counseling exceptions, uses vague 'responsible parenting' phrasing, and permits K-4 gender discussions via student-initiated questions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Resist, delay, or narrow Policy 1310 changes to uphold DPS's gender support policy and protect LGBTQIA+ students and educators.
side_b_arguments: Requiring staff to notify parents of pronoun/name changes outs vulnerable students and erodes trust with educators.

Restricting K-4 classroom discussions marginalizes trans kindergartners and families with same-sex parents, while Parker v. Hurley precedent rejects claims that inclusive curriculum burdens parental rights.
conflicts.resolution: Public hearing for feedback only; no board action taken at this session.

conflicts.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 9/22/22
conflicts.issue: City of Durham Request to Mount ShotSpotter Acoustic Sensors on DPS School Buildings
conflicts.summary: Board members debated a City of Durham request for an MOA allowing ShotSpotter gunshot detection devices to be mounted on school parapet walls, weighing intergovernmental deference and potential response-time benefits against student surveillance concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Decline mounting ShotSpotter surveillance devices on school buildings and focus city-school partnerships on root causes of gun violence.
side_a_arguments: Placing acoustic surveillance equipment on school buildings sends an undesirable message to students and represents excessive surveillance.
Other mounting locations exist for the city's already-approved project, making school buildings unnecessary.
Collaboration with the city should prioritize addressing the root causes of gun violence, and some expressed interest in a buffer zone around schools.
conflicts.side_b_position: Respect the City Council's approved ShotSpotter pilot and consider potential emergency response-time benefits.
side_b_arguments: Durham City Council already voted to approve ShotSpotter, and inter-body collaboration favors deferring to the city's judgment on its program.
Acoustic detection could provide single-digit-second improvements in emergency response time if shots are fired near a school.
conflicts.resolution: Board Attorney Rod Malone advised that a motion was only needed to move forward with an MOA, not to decline it. No board member made a motion to proceed, so the administration took no action to place ShotSpotter devices on DPS schools.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, Agenda Amendment, and May 9 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The work session opened with a moment of silence reflecting on the end of the school year, graduations, the Board of County Commissioners' budget investment, Pride Month, and community violence. On a motion by Jovonia Lewis, seconded by Millicent Rogers, the board removed Consent Item 2A (crosswalk and sidewalk contract at Lyons Farm Elementary School) to Discussion Item 4B and approved the amended agenda, then approved the May 9, 2024 meeting minutes on a motion by Natalie Beyer and Millicent Rogers.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (agenda amendment, amended agenda, and May 9 minutes)

agenda_items.title: General Public Comment and County Budget Appreciation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Two public commenters addressed the board: parent Mary Elizabeth Hanchi recounted pulling her medically fragile child from DPS after inconsistent school nurse coverage at Creekside Elementary left her child without protocol support during heat exposure, and John Hodges-Copple of Durham for DSA urged DPS to protect funding for elementary schools alongside DSA transformation and provide written documentation. Following public comment, Jessica Carda-Auten and Interim Superintendent Catty Moore thanked Durham County Commissioners for funding $27.3 million of DPS's $27.5 million request (98%) for classified and certified staff compensation, hard-to-staff supplements, capital outlay, and Pre-K, while acknowledging pending state budget questions.

agenda_items.title: Immigrant Student Protections, Policy 5120, and School Naming Feedback
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the transcript, board members and Chief Legal Officer Dr. Tanya Giovanni discussed converting the board's resolution protecting immigrant students and families regardless of status into an accessible, bilingual annual back-to-school flyer alongside annual staff training. Members also discussed pending state legislation (referencing HB 10 and SB 49), differences between grievances and complaints, potential review of Policy 5120 (Relationship with Law Enforcement), and a June 14–24 public feedback window on proposed school names (including whether to use 'health' or 'medicine').

agenda_items.title: Item 4B: Linear Construction Contract for Lyons Farm Elementary Crosswalk and Sidewalk
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained that the Lyons Farm Elementary crosswalk and sidewalk addition was deferred after the school's 2022 completion to avoid delaying opening during concurrent site-plan reviews, and would now use capital outlay funds for safe routes to school. Board members questioned why DPS capital outlay rather than the City of Durham or NCDOT was bearing offsite road-improvement costs and what precedent that set for upcoming bond-funded elementary schools, while weighing the risk of bids expiring if delayed until December. After members affirmed that safety and not losing the active bid required moving forward, the board voted 6-0 to approve the contract while calling for City of Durham financial support on future projects.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session and June 13, 2024 Personnel Action Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted 6-0 on a motion by Millicent Rogers, seconded by Natalie Beyer, to enter closed session for reasons stated on the agenda. Returning to open session at 05:16:24, the board unanimously approved the June 13, 2024 Personnel Action Report on a motion by Natalie Beyer, seconded by Emily Chávez, and adjourned.

meetings.title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Called Meeting | 5/28/24
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of Education held a special called meeting on May 28, 2024, centered on the superintendent search. After amending the agenda and holding a 45-minute closed personnel session, the board heard a public presentation from Alma Advisory Group summarizing community engagement, survey demographics, and search priorities across ~93 EEO-surveyed applicants. Key Alma findings highlighted universal priority on attracting and retaining staff, rebuilding trust—especially among classified staff and underserved families—and student prioritization of school safety, while recommending no changes to the superintendent job profile. The board then entered a second hour-long closed personnel session and reconvened briefly at 02:47:50 to schedule additional Saturday interviews from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Agenda Amendment, and Initial Closed Session (Personnel)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Bettina Umstead called the special meeting on the superintendent search to order at 00:00:55. Emily Chávez moved and Natalie Beyer seconded amending the agenda to add an opening closed session for personnel, which passed unanimously, followed by a unanimous vote on Natalie Beyer's motion (seconded by Emily Chávez) to enter closed session for approximately 45 minutes.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Agenda amendment passed (unanimous); Closed session passed (unanimous)

agenda_items.title: Alma Advisory Group Community Engagement Report on Superintendent Search
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning to open session at 00:48:25, Alma Advisory Group presenters (Eliana and Naja) reported on the superintendent search applicant pool (including 93 self-reported EEO survey responses) and community engagement findings. They highlighted strong community support for district equity work, universal top priorities on staff recruitment/retention and rebuilding trust (including classified staff trust concerns and high engagement needs among Hispanic/Latino, Black, LGBTQIA+, and neurodivergent/disability communities), student emphasis on school safety, and alignment with the existing job profile. Board members thanked Alma and emphasized repairing trust with classified employees and multilingual families.

agenda_items.title: Second Closed Session (Personnel) and Interview Schedule Addition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: At 01:45:08, Millicent Rogers moved and another member seconded entering a second closed session for personnel matters, which passed unanimously. Returning to open session at 02:47:50, the board confirmed adding extra interview time on Saturday from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM before adjourning at 02:48:29.

meetings.title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 5/23/24
meetings.executive_summary: At a seven-hour monthly meeting on May 23, 2024, the Board of Education navigated intense labor and facilities advocacy alongside unanimous approvals of consent items and the Perkins V Career and Technical Education (CTE) local application. Interim Superintendent Kathy Moore detailed FY 2024-25 local budget austerity measures and confirmed construction of the new Durham School of the Arts (DSA) at Duke Homestead is moving forward, while Chair Bettina Umstead reported on the Meet and Confer Ad Hoc Committee after DAE members walked out of the May 20 committee session. Dozens of Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) interpreters (who staged a coordinated day off), DAE and allied union members, and Durham for DSA speakers pressed the board on pay cuts, sole union recognition, and downtown DSA renovation. Following a presentation on individual salary projection statements and a first draft of a Salary Administration Policy—where Natalie Beyer questioned displaying erroneous Hill Study figures—the board held a nearly three-hour closed session and approved the personnel report 5-0 with one abstention (Jovonia Lewis absent).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, and Celebrations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Bettina Umstead called the monthly meeting to order with Jovonia Lewis attending virtually and led a moment of silence. Staff recognized DSA senior Evan Byers as Student of the Month, Northern High School's Southeast Regional Junior Chef champions, 32 NC Governor's School selectees, 10 Magnet Schools of America national award schools, May Teacher of the Month Holly McLam (Glenn), May Employee of the Month Sabas Peña Ortiz (Rogers-Herr), and Employees of Distinction including Teacher of the Year First Sergeant Jeffrey Matthews (Hillside).

agenda_items.title: Superintendent's Update and Meet & Confer Ad Hoc Committee Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Superintendent Kathy Moore announced Bull City Teaching Scholars recipients and Project SEARCH graduates, outlined FY 2024-25 local budget cuts (eliminating beyond-formula school allotments, tightening emergency/EPP licensure payroll, freezing local expenditures, and reviewing non-school hiring), and stated staff is moving forward with the new DSA at Duke Homestead based on standing unanimous board approval. Chair Umstead then updated the board on the Meet and Confer Ad Hoc Committee, noting four open meetings had been held, DAE-appointed members walked out before the May 20 meeting convened, and remaining members continued drafting policy including Teamsters feedback.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Review and Approval of March 21 and April 25, 2024 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board unanimously approved the May 23, 2024 meeting agenda and then approved the regular monthly meeting minutes from March 21 and April 25, 2024, on a motion by Natalie Beyer and second by Jessica Carda-Auten.

agenda_items.title: General Public Comment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Over an hour of public comment (one-minute limit) centered on three fronts: DHH ASL interpreters and language facilitators protesting ~$932/month pay reductions via a May 23 coordinated day off and warning of IDEA/ADA IEP compliance risks; DAE educators, allied unions (NNU, UE 150, AFGE, IBEW, UNITE HERE, USSW, Duke Grad Student Union), and parents demanding sole recognition of DAE in a Meet and Confer policy while denouncing non-union ad hoc committee seats; and Durham for DSA advocates urging in-place downtown renovation to save $50–$85 million for elementary school repairs, alongside TA-to-Teacher tuition and Growing Together transfer complaints.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items A–N)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Board members approved consent agenda items A through N as reviewed in advance, on a motion by Natalie Beyer and second by Millicent Rogers with no items pulled for discussion.

agenda_items.title: Academic Services: Career and Technical Education (CTE) Local Application
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Julie Pack and Darian Harris presented Perkins V CTE performance outcomes—including 9,586 grade 6–12 participants, a 99% concentrator graduation rate, >95% postsecondary placement across subgroups, and the 8th-grade Career Accelerator—alongside plans to pilot comprehensive career exploration across middle schools. Board members praised the program and unanimously approved the 2024-25 CTE local application on a motion by Alexandra Valladares and second by Natalie Beyer.

agenda_items.title: Salary Projections Update and Draft Salary Administration Policy Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a brief recess, Interim Superintendent Moore, consultant Mr. Crutchfield, Dr. Alvera Lesane, and CLO Dr. Tanya Giovanni reviewed upcoming individual electronic salary projections (incorporating 60% pay ranges at Grade 61+ within the $8.8M classified request) and presented the first draft of an overarching Salary Administration Policy and forthcoming Regulations & Procedures (R&P). Board members debated whether displaying erroneous Hill Study figures on employee statements would cause harm, examined why DHH interpreters saw ~$900/month drops relative to private contracting rates, and urged adding a 4–6 year salary study cadence, extra-duty parity, promotion rules, and mobile-accessible office hours.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session and May 23, 2024 Personnel Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: At 04:11:38, the board voted 7-0 by roll call to enter closed session for nearly three hours. Returning to open session at 07:03:22 with Jovonia Lewis absent, the board approved the May 23, 2024 personnel report by a 5-0 vote with one abstention before adjourning.

disagreements.meeting_title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Monthly Meeting | 5/23/24
disagreements.issue: Inclusion of Erroneous Hill Study Salary Figures in Employee Projection Statements
disagreements.summary: During discussion of upcoming electronic salary projection documents, Natalie Beyer argued against displaying the flawed Hill Study salary amounts, while Interim Superintendent Kathy Moore defended including them for direct historical comparison.
disagreements.side_a_position: Omit erroneous Hill Study salary figures from employee projection statements to avoid causing further confusion and harm.
side_a_arguments: Some job categories in the Hill Study contained erroneous rates that misled employees about realistic pay.
Re-publishing erroneous consultant numbers causes distress when staff thought those rates were settled.
disagreements.side_b_position: Include the Hill Study column alongside 2022-23, current 2022-23 + 11%, and proposed Crutchfield schedules for transparency.
side_b_arguments: The Hill Study schedules were formally voted on by the board and actually paid to employees for three to four months.
Employees expect a direct comparison explaining why Hill rates differed from market rates and current proposals.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion only; administration indicated plans to include the Hill column with explanatory caveats and a dispute/FAQ portal.

disagreements.issue: Meet and Confer Ad Hoc Committee Structure vs. Sole Recognition of DAE
disagreements.summary: Public speakers representing DAE and allied labor unions fiercely criticized the board's ad hoc committee for including non-union appointees and delayed union recognition, while Chair Bettina Umstead defended the collaborative multi-stakeholder committee.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the multi-stakeholder Meet and Confer Ad Hoc Committee incorporating DAE, Teamsters, and non-union employees under NC legal constraints.
side_a_arguments: North Carolina law creates unique legal constraints requiring collaborative policy design.
Board seeks input from employees across all work sites and roles, including non-union staff and other employee organizations like Teamsters, without creating division.
disagreements.side_b_position: Immediately adopt a Meet and Confer policy formally recognizing DAE as sole representative of DPS workers.
side_b_arguments: DAE represents over 2,700 workers (more than half of DPS staff) and is the only democratically elected majority union.
Board-appointed non-union seats on the ad hoc committee undermine majority worker voice and stall formal recognition.
disagreements.resolution: No formal board vote taken; DAE-appointed members left the May 20 committee meeting prior to convening while the ad hoc committee remained active.

meetings.title: #DPSCommunity | DPS Board of Education Special Called Meeting | 5/13/24
meetings.executive_summary: Vice Chair Emily Chávez presided in person over a Special Called Meeting with Alma Advisory Group consultants Monica Rosen and Naja Thompson to advance the superintendent search, while Chair Bettina Umstead participated virtually and Board Member Jovonia Lewis joined after the opening agenda vote. The Board unanimously approved confidentiality agreements for incoming board members Wendell Tabb and Harrell, waived Board Policy 2302 restrictions on wholly remote meetings for candidate interviews, and adopted a four-round screening process. Following extensive debate balancing public transparency against sitting-superintendent applicant confidentiality, the Board unanimously approved an amended compromise structure using confidential, NDA-bound community panels during the finalist round without publicly naming non-selected finalists.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, and Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Emily Chávez called the meeting to order with Bettina Umstead joining virtually and Jovonia Lewis arriving shortly thereafter. Following a moment of silence, the Board approved the meeting agenda by roll call vote.

agenda_items.title: Superintendent Search Status, Recruitment Pipeline, and Community Engagement Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Alma Advisory Group consultants Monica Rosen and Naja Thompson reviewed recent Durham site-visit listening sessions, focus groups, and survey outreach along with early applicant sourcing metrics. Board members asked questions regarding outreach equity, translation access, and timeline milestones ahead of screening.

agenda_items.title: Confidentiality Agreements for Incoming Board Members
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board discussed when and how incoming board members Wendell Tabb and Harrell should join executive screening sessions prior to taking office. After legal guidance on confidentiality obligations, the Board authorized Tharrington Smith to execute confidentiality agreements with the incoming members.

agenda_items.title: Waiver of Board Policy 2302 for Wholly Remote Candidate Interviews
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Alma Advisory Group recommended conducting early-round superintendent screening interviews virtually to accommodate working candidates and tight scheduling. The Board voted to waive Section B.2 of Board Policy 2302 restricting wholly remote board meetings for the interview rounds.

agenda_items.title: Four-Round Superintendent Screening Process and Timeline (Slide 14)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Board members reviewed the multi-stage candidate vetting roadmap from initial Alma screening through Round 2 video interviews, Round 3 live interviews beginning June 3-7 with incoming board members included, and final selection.

agenda_items.title: Finalist Round Community Engagement and Confidentiality Structure
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Board members held a sustained debate between an open public finalist visit (Option A) and a confidential finalist process utilizing NDA-bound community stakeholder panels (Option B). After hearing that sitting superintendents had expressed reluctance to apply under a public finalist model, the Board amended and unanimously approved Option B.

votes.item_title: Approve Special Called Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Jovonia Lewis had not yet arrived at the time of the opening roll call vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Vice Chair Emily Chávez called the May 13, 2024 special meeting to order, noting that Chair Bettina Umstead was participating remotely and Board Member Jovonia Lewis would join momentarily. Millicent Rogers moved to approve the agenda as presented, and Alexandra Valladares seconded the motion. No revisions or objections were raised by members. The Board approved the agenda 6-0 via roll call vote.

votes.item_title: Authorize Tharrington Smith to Execute Confidentiality Agreements with Incoming Board Members (Wendell Tabb and Harrell)
votes.notes: Jovonia Lewis arrived prior to this vote, bringing attendance to all 7 board members.
votes.discussion_detail: Alma Advisory Group raised the question of how incoming board members Wendell Tabb and Harrell should be integrated into the superintendent selection timeline so the future board feels ownership over the hire. Board members discussed legal risks around personnel privacy under North Carolina law if non-seated individuals view confidential application materials before taking office. With input from counsel and Alma, members agreed that executing formal non-disclosure agreements would safeguard candidate privacy while allowing incoming members to participate at Round 3. Millicent Rogers moved and Natalie Beyer seconded authorizing Tharrington Smith to execute those confidentiality agreements, passing 7-0 on roll call.

votes.item_title: Waive Board Policy 2302 (Section B.2 Restriction on Wholly Remote Meetings) for Superintendent Candidate Interviews
votes.notes: Allows virtual closed-session interviews during early screening rounds.
votes.discussion_detail: Alma consultants advised that conducting initial candidate interviews virtually reduces travel barriers and protects applicant confidentiality during working hours. Because Board Policy 2302 Section B.2 limits wholly remote board meetings, members reviewed whether a narrow policy waiver was appropriate for executive screening sessions. Members voiced broad consensus that virtual access would maximize scheduling flexibility and maintain a strong applicant pool. Natalie Beyer moved to waive Section B.2 of Policy 2302 for the interview process, seconded by Millicent Rogers, and the motion carried 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Four-Round Superintendent Screening Process (Slide 14)
votes.notes: Clarified that incoming board members will join at Round 3 (June 3-7).
votes.discussion_detail: Monica Rosen walked the Board through Slide 14 detailing the four screening stages, including consultant vetting, video essays, semi-finalist interviews, and finalist assessments. Board members clarified logistics and confirmed that incoming board members who sign confidentiality agreements will join the deliberations starting in Round 3 during the week of June 3 through June 7. Members appreciated the structured rubric tied to the Board's competency framework. Jessica Carda-Auten moved to approve the four-round screening process, Millicent Rogers seconded, and it passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Confidential Finalist Round Structure with NDA Community Engagement Panels (Amended Motion)
votes.notes: Compromise resolved debate between Option A (public) and Option B (confidential NDA panel).
votes.discussion_detail: Millicent Rogers initially moved, seconded by Emily Chávez, to adopt an open public finalist visit (Option A) so the broader Durham community could meet top candidates in person, arguing transparency helps rebuild community trust. However, Monica Rosen warned that two active applicants and one prospective candidate—specifically sitting superintendents—had already expressed discomfort with public finalist naming due to career risk in their current districts. Natalie Beyer and Jovonia Lewis argued strongly for Option B, stressing that preserving confidentiality protects the strongest sitting-superintendent pool while still engaging 10 to 12 representative community panelists bound by confidentiality agreements. Chair Bettina Umstead emphasized wanting both community voice and the strongest possible candidate slate. Following extensive deliberation, Millicent Rogers amended her motion—accepted by Emily Chávez—to adopt confidential NDA-protected community finalist panels without public naming, which passed unanimously 7-0.

disagreements.issue: Publicly Named Finalist Visits (Option A) vs. Confidential NDA Community Panels (Option B)
disagreements.summary: Board members debated whether superintendent finalists should be publicly announced for open community forums (Option A) or interviewed in closed sessions with confidential community stakeholder panels signing non-disclosure agreements (Option B).
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold an open public finalist round so all Durham stakeholders can vet and engage finalists transparently.
side_a_arguments: Public forums help rebuild community trust after recent district turmoil.
Board leadership originally signaled openness and broad community participation in finalist vetting.
disagreements.side_b_position: Use confidential finalist community panels under signed NDAs without publicly naming non-selected finalists.
